description: A family of secreted adaptor proteins that bridge presynaptic neurexins to postsynaptic ligands. In this text, they function as synaptic organizers with isoform-specific binding partners and effects on receptor regulation and synapse properties.

Presynaptic cell-adhesion molecules that bind cerebellins to form trans-synaptic complexes. They are central components of the described synaptic signaling pathways and determine downstream effects depending on isoform and ligand pairing.

Postsynaptic ligands that interact with cerebellin-neurexin complexes, especially Cbln1-3-associated complexes. They participate in organizing synaptic properties and receptor regulation in specific brain regions.
A postsynaptic ligand that binds Cbln4 in neurexin/cerebellin complexes. It is part of the signaling axis implicated in perforant-path synaptic plasticity.
A postsynaptic ligand that partners with Cbln4 in neurexin/cerebellin complexes. It contributes to synaptic regulation, particularly in perforant-path synapses and LTP.
A specific trans-synaptic molecular complex that organizes cerebellar parallel-fiber synapses. It represents a classical example of cerebellin-neurexin-mediated synaptic specification.
A synaptic complex in the hippocampal subiculum and prefrontal cortex that upregulates postsynaptic NMDA receptors. It exemplifies isoform-specific regulation of synaptic receptor composition.

A synaptic complex in the hippocampal subiculum and prefrontal cortex that downregulates postsynaptic AMPA receptors. It demonstrates that different neurexin isoforms can drive opposite receptor-level outcomes.

A synaptic complex at perforant-path synapses that is essential for long-term potentiation. It does not alter basal synaptic transmission or NMDA/AMPA receptor levels, indicating a selective role in plasticity.

A specific synaptic setting in the cerebellum where neurexin-Cbln1-GluD2 complexes organize synaptic properties. It serves as the classical anatomical context for cerebellin-mediated synapse organization.
A brain region where Nrxn1-Cbln2-GluD1 complexes upregulate postsynaptic NMDA receptors. It is one of the extra-cerebellar synaptic contexts discussed in the abstract.

A brain region where Nrxn1-Cbln2-GluD1 complexes upregulate postsynaptic NMDA receptors and Nrxn3-Cbln2-GluD1 complexes downregulate postsynaptic AMPA receptors. It is a key extra-cerebellar site of synaptic regulation.

A synaptic setting in the dentate gyrus where neurexin/Cbln4/Neogenin-1 complexes are essential for LTP. It is notable for plasticity dependence without changes in basal transmission or receptor abundance.
A hippocampal region containing perforant-path synapses where neurexin/Cbln4/Neogenin-1 complexes support LTP. It provides the anatomical context for the described plasticity mechanism.

Postsynaptic glutamate receptors whose abundance is increased by Nrxn1-Cbln2-GluD1 complexes in the hippocampal subiculum and prefrontal cortex. They are downstream effectors of synaptic complex signaling.

Postsynaptic glutamate receptors whose abundance is decreased by Nrxn3-Cbln2-GluD1 complexes in the hippocampal subiculum and prefrontal cortex. They are downstream targets of synaptic complex-mediated regulation.
Long-term potentiation, a synaptic plasticity process essential for strengthening synaptic transmission. In this text, it depends on neurexin/Cbln4/Neogenin-1 complexes at perforant-path synapses.
The developmental process of establishing synaptic contacts. The abstract states that the described cerebellin-neurexin signaling pathways are not required for this process.
The baseline level of synaptic signaling under resting conditions. In perforant-path synapses, neurexin/Cbln4/Neogenin-1 complexes do not affect this process.
A synaptic plasticity process in the hippocampus that is central to learning and memory; in this text it is the primary biological outcome whose induction is being mechanistically dissected.
Higher-order cognitive outcomes that are thought to depend on hippocampal LTP; included as the functional endpoint motivating the study.
A key neuronal kinase implicated in LTP induction; the paper contrasts its enzymatic activity with its structural role in synaptic signaling.
The catalytic function of CaMKII that had been widely assumed to be required for LTP induction, but is challenged here as the primary mechanism.
Non-catalytic functions of CaMKII that support LTP induction, especially through protein-protein interactions rather than kinase activity.

entity_name: BINDING TO THE NMDA-TYPE GLUTAMATE RECEPTOR SUBUNIT GLUN2B
description: A structural interaction between CaMKII and GluN2B that is highlighted as a critical non-enzymatic mechanism supporting LTP.
A receptor subunit that interacts with CaMKII and serves as a molecular partner in the structural mechanism underlying LTP induction.
Experimental tools used to selectively manipulate CaMKII functions and distinguish enzymatic from structural contributions to LTP.
A CaMKII phosphorylation event that autoregulates the structural role of CaMKII and helps explain the separation between catalytic and structural functions.
The catalytic activity of CaMKII referred to in the paper as contributing only indirectly by autoregulating the structural role via T286 autophosphorylation.
A strong LTP induction outcome observed when the structural function of CaMKII is directly initiated, even under conditions where enzymatic activity is blocked.
The catalytic activity of CaMKII specifically discussed as being blocked in experiments and shown not to be sufficient for LTP induction.

A synaptic plasticity process discussed as the central phenomenon of the review. It is characterized by changes in synaptic strength, with threshold and magnitude influenced by multiple proteins, and is driven in the core mechanism by NMDA receptor activation followed by CaMKII activation.
A broad set of proteins implicated in LTP. The text emphasizes that many of these proteins are not essential for LTP itself but can modulate its threshold and/or magnitude, often indirectly.
A glutamate receptor required for the initiation of the core LTP mechanism. Its activation is described as the first necessary step preceding CaMKII activation.

Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, identified as a required downstream activator in LTP. Its activation leads to rapid recruitment of AMPA receptors to the synapse and is linked to PSD modifications.

Ionotropic glutamate receptors that are rapidly recruited to the synapse following CaMKII activation. Their recruitment is independent of subunit type but requires an adequate pool of surface receptors.
The subcellular site where AMPA receptors are rapidly recruited during LTP. It is the functional location at which synaptic strengthening is expressed.
A molecular attribute of AMPA receptors noted as not determining the recruitment response in this context. The text states that AMPA receptor recruitment is independent of subunit type.
The available pool of receptors at the cell surface required for rapid AMPA receptor enrichment at the synapse. Adequate abundance is necessary for the recruitment process described in LTP.
The postsynaptic density, a synaptic molecular structure that undergoes modifications downstream of CaMKII activation to permit rapid AMPA receptor enrichment.
The special-issue thematic context referenced by the article, representing a broader class of synaptic plasticity mechanisms dependent on glutamate receptor signaling.

Long-term potentiation, a synaptic plasticity process central to learning and memory. In this text it is the main biological process whose induction, intermediary expression phase, and maintenance are being dissected mechanistically.
Higher-order cognitive processes discussed as depending on the induction and maintenance of LTP. It provides the functional context for the mechanistic findings.

Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, a signaling kinase required for LTP induction and implicated here in autonomous enzymatic activity during post-induction LTP expression. It functions through structural and enzymatic roles and interacts with GluN2B.
The full name of CaMKII, a kinase described as necessary for LTP induction and as the source of autonomous activity after binding to GluN2B.

The NMDA-type glutamate receptor subunit that binds CaMKII and regulates its structural function. This interaction generates Ca2+-independent autonomous CaMKII activity and is central to post-induction LTP expression.
The receptor subunit class to which GluN2B belongs. It provides the molecular receptor context for CaMKII binding in the described mechanism.
Ca2+-independent enzymatic activity of CaMKII generated by binding to GluN2B. It is dispensable for early LTP induction but required for the subsequent intermediary phase of LTP expression.
The initial phase of long-term potentiation establishment. The text states that this phase requires CaMKII but not its enzymatic autonomous activity.
The phase of LTP following induction, including an intermediary phase within about 15 minutes. It is the process mediated by autonomous CaMKII activity in the study.
A temporally defined post-induction phase of LTP expression occurring within about 15 minutes. The study identifies this phase as requiring autonomous CaMKII activity.
The later phase of sustaining potentiation after expression. The text suggests it may depend on structural functions of GluN2B-bound CaMKII but not on the resulting enzymatic activity.
Non-enzymatic functions of CaMKII emphasized as important for LTP induction and possibly later maintenance. These functions are distinguished from autonomous enzymatic activity.
A specific CaMKII regulatory modification mentioned as not being the mechanism through which autonomous CaMKII activity mediates post-induction LTP.
A molecular assembly behavior mentioned as not required for the autonomous CaMKII activity-mediated post-induction LTP effect, particularly in the context of later maintenance.

Ca(2+)/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, a signaling kinase highlighted as a key molecular regulator in the induction of long-term potentiation. In the abstract, its activation is described as both necessary and sufficient for LTP induction, making it a central upstream molecular feature in the mechanism under discussion.

A synaptic plasticity process discussed as the main biological phenomenon of interest. The text emphasizes its induction and the molecular mechanisms underlying it, particularly downstream of CaMKII activation.

Abbreviation for long-term potentiation, the same synaptic strengthening process referenced throughout the abstract. It is the endpoint biological process whose induction is linked to CaMKII activation.

The intracellular and signaling mechanisms that mediate LTP induction downstream of CaMKII activation. This is a broad mechanistic process category used in the review to frame current understanding and open questions.
The full descriptive form of CaMKII as a calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase. It identifies the molecular feature responsible for initiating signaling events relevant to LTP induction.

Cultured neuronal preparation used as the experimental subject/population in which long-term potentiation-related molecular and cellular changes are studied. It provides an in vitro model for dissecting synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
Dissociated hippocampal neuron culture system used as a model population for studying NMDA receptor-dependent long-term potentiation and synaptic plasticity.
Hippocampal CA1 neuronal population used as an in vivo/in situ reference for comparing long-term potentiation properties with cultured neuronal models.
Ex vivo hippocampal tissue preparation used to study long-term potentiation with electrophysiological techniques and to benchmark cultured neuron plasticity models.
A form of synaptic plasticity characterized by persistent enhancement of excitatory synaptic transmission that depends on NMDA receptor signaling and downstream calcium-dependent mechanisms.

entity_name: PERSISTENT ENHANCEMENT OF EXCITATORY SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
description: Functional strengthening of excitatory synaptic signaling that serves as the physiological manifestation of long-term potentiation in neuronal cultures and hippocampal tissue.

entity_name: CA(2+) INFLUX THROUGH POST-SYNAPTIC NMDA RECEPTORS
description: Calcium entry through postsynaptic NMDA receptors that initiates signaling cascades required for long-term potentiation in hippocampal neurons.

entity_name: ACTIVATION AND AUTOPHOSPHORYLATION OF THE CA(2+)/CALMODULIN-DEPENDENT PROTEIN KINASE II (CAMKII)
description: Downstream calcium-dependent signaling event involving activation and autophosphorylation of CaMKII, a key step in long-term potentiation induction and maintenance.

entity_name: INCREASE IN ALPHA-AMINO-3-HYDROXY-5-METHYLISOXAZOLE-4-PROPIONATE (AMPA) RECEPTOR INSERTION AT THE POST-SYNAPTIC MEMBRANE
description: Activity-dependent trafficking process in which AMPA receptors are inserted into the postsynaptic membrane, strengthening synaptic transmission during long-term potentiation.

entity_name: RECRUITMENT OF AMPA RECEPTORS AT THE POSTSYNAPTIC SITE
description: Synaptic trafficking process central to long-term potentiation, involving accumulation of AMPA receptors at postsynaptic membranes to enhance excitatory signaling.
Native receptor proteins located postsynaptically whose changes are monitored in cultured neuron models to study long-term potentiation-associated signaling and receptor trafficking.
Intracellular pathways underlying long-term potentiation and activity-induced synaptic modification in cultured hippocampal neurons.
Neuronal activity input that controls a neuron's capacity to modify synapses during long-term potentiation.
Endogenous AMPA-type glutamate receptors studied in cultured hippocampal neurons as targets of activity-dependent trafficking during long-term potentiation.
Experimental methods used to assess synaptic function and long-term potentiation in hippocampal slices and neuronal cultures.
Protocol classes used to induce persistent synaptic enhancement in cultured hippocampal neurons and characterize plasticity models.
In vitro model systems based on cultured neurons used to investigate mechanisms of synaptic plasticity and receptor trafficking.

Ex vivo hippocampal tissue culture model used as the experimental subject/population in which synaptic plasticity mechanisms were studied. It provides a controlled neural preparation for examining molecular regulation of LTP and LTD.

The activity-dependent process by which synaptic strength is modified; in this paper it is the central biological process under investigation and is described as bidirectional, encompassing both potentiation and depression.

A form of synaptic plasticity characterized by persistent strengthening of synaptic transmission. In the abstract, it is one of the two major bidirectional plasticity outcomes and is linked to RCAN1 phosphorylation at a PKA site.

A form of synaptic plasticity characterized by persistent weakening of synaptic transmission. In the abstract, it is one of the two major bidirectional plasticity outcomes and is associated with RCAN1 phosphorylation by GSK3β.
Higher-order functional neural outcome described as being underpinned by synaptic plasticity. It represents the physiological significance of the mechanisms studied in the paper.

A phosphatase whose activity is bidirectionally regulated in the study. It is the key molecular target whose activation state is controlled by RCAN1 phosphorylation and is central to LTD and LTP induction.

Endogenous regulator-of-calcineurin protein identified as a molecular switch for bidirectional synaptic plasticity. Its phosphorylation state determines whether calcineurin is activated or blocked, thereby influencing LTD versus LTP.
A kinase that phosphorylates RCAN1 in the mechanism described. Its action on RCAN1 underlies calcineurin activation and is necessary for LTD induction.
Protein kinase A, referenced as the kinase acting at a PKA site on RCAN1. Phosphorylation at this site blocks calcineurin activity and supports LTP induction.

A persistent increase in synaptic strength used here as the cellular model for learning and memory. The text distinguishes its induction from its maintenance and identifies it as the process whose maintenance depends on CaMKII.
The acquisition phase of memory-related synaptic change, referenced as the induction phase of LTP. It is used in the abstract to contrast with memory maintenance.
The persistence phase of synaptic plasticity, referenced as the maintenance phase of LTP. The paper argues that CaMKII is required for this maintenance process.

A calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase implicated as a key molecular regulator of synaptic transmission and LTP maintenance. The abstract reports that acute inhibition erases LTP and transient inhibition enhances subsequent LTP, supporting a role as a molecular storage device.
The process of signal transfer across synapses, reported here to be contributed to by CaMKII. It is part of the functional synaptic context in which LTP is maintained.
A short-term experimental perturbation that suppresses CaMKII activity. In the abstract, this intervention erases LTP, indicating CaMKII dependence of LTP maintenance.
A temporary inhibition of CaMKII used experimentally to probe plasticity dynamics. The text reports that it enhances subsequent LTP, suggesting a priming or metaplastic effect.

A conceptual functional model proposed for CaMKII, describing it as a molecular mechanism that stores synaptic memory information. It is not a quantitative metric but a domain-relevant interpretive framework.

A calcium/calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine protein kinase discussed as the central molecular entity in the abstract. It is described as a memory-associated kinase with notable structural and regulatory properties, and it is implicated in neuronal plasticity processes including long-term potentiation, long-term depression, and memory storage.

A broader family of calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases that includes CaMKII. In the text, this family provides the contextual framework for comparing CaMKII with related kinases and highlights functional diversity within the kinase group.

A synaptic plasticity process associated with strengthening of neuronal connections. The abstract notes that CaMKII's involvement in LTP was established early and helped support its reputation as a memory molecule.
A synaptic plasticity process associated with weakening of neuronal connections. The abstract states that CaMKII's neuronal functions extend to LTD, indicating a broader role in synaptic regulation.
The biological process of encoding and maintaining memory information. The abstract reports direct evidence supporting CaMKII as a contributor to memory storage.

A functional designation for a molecule implicated in memory-related neuronal processes. In the abstract, CaMKII is described as having been touted as a memory molecule, reflecting its proposed role in memory mechanisms.

Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, a highly abundant brain kinase that mediates hippocampal long-term potentiation and is implicated in both normal synaptic plasticity and pathological LTP impairments in Alzheimer's disease and global cerebral ischemia.
A form of synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus that is prominently mediated by CaMKII and is considered important for learning and memory.
The broader neuronal process encompassing long-term potentiation and related changes in synaptic strength, described here as a mechanism required for learning and memory.
A cognitive functional endpoint associated with hippocampal long-term potentiation and impaired in the pathological conditions discussed in the abstract.
Deficits in long-term potentiation observed in pathological contexts; these impairments are linked to Alzheimer's disease, global cerebral ischemia, and altered CaMKII function.
A neurodegenerative disease condition associated in the abstract with pathological LTP impairments mediated by CaMKII.
A brain ischemic condition associated with pathological LTP impairments and CaMKII-mediated dysfunction.
Inhibitory agents targeting CaMKII that prevented the LTP impairments described for Alzheimer's disease and global cerebral ischemia.
A physiological aging context in which milder LTP impairments occur through passive loss of CaMKII function rather than active pathological mechanisms.
A mechanism of reduced CaMKII activity described as the basis for milder LTP impairments in normal aging.

Ca2+/CaM-dependent protein kinase II, a dodecameric kinase complex central to synaptic plasticity. In this review it is described as having both enzymatic and structural functions, with abundant expression in neuronal cells and diverse interacting partners, making it a key molecular regulator of long-term potentiation.

The full molecular name of CaMKII, referring to the calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II complex. It functions as a kinase in phosphorylation-dependent signaling and is implicated in the regulation of long-term potentiation.
A persistent form of synaptic strengthening that underlies learning and memory. The text identifies it as the biological process in which CaMKII plays pivotal, necessary, and sufficient roles.
Abbreviation for long-term potentiation, the same synaptic plasticity process discussed in the article. It is used as the primary functional endpoint for CaMKII activity in neurons.

The collection of molecular components that regulate plasticity in neurons. CaMKII is described as one of the most extensively studied components of this machinery in the context of long-term potentiation.

A broad biological process referring to the ability of neurons and synapses to change their strength or structure. The article frames CaMKII as a regulator of plasticity, especially synaptic plasticity.
Activity-dependent changes in synaptic function. The text states that CaMKII's enzymatic and structural functions cooperate in the induction of this process.

Morphological remodeling of synapses, including changes in dendritic spine structure. The article indicates that CaMKII contributes to its induction through cooperative enzymatic and structural roles.
Specialized postsynaptic neuronal protrusions whose structure changes during synaptic plasticity. In the text, they are the structural site where CaMKII contributes to plasticity-related remodeling.
The cellular population in which CaMKII is described as extraordinarily abundant. These cells provide the biological context for CaMKII's enzymatic and structural roles in synaptic plasticity.
Molecular targets phosphorylated by CaMKII. They represent the downstream substrates through which CaMKII exerts its kinase activity in long-term potentiation.
Molecules that interact with CaMKII and are cited as supporting its proposed structural roles. Their diversity is used as evidence for CaMKII's non-enzymatic functions.

A calcium/calmodulin-regulated phosphatase discussed as a key signaling enzyme in dendritic spines. It is localized by interactions with scaffold and synaptic proteins and responds to smaller Ca2+ influxes through NMDARs to promote long-term depression.

A highly abundant neuronal kinase (CaMKII) that is activated by calmodulin at similar Ca2+ concentrations as calcineurin. In dendritic spines, its activity drives long-term synaptic potentiation following large Ca2+ influxes through NMDARs.
Abbreviation for calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, a major synaptic signaling kinase whose localization and activation are central to potentiation in dendritic spines.
A calcium-binding regulatory protein that activates calcineurin and CaMKII at similar Ca2+ concentrations in vitro, thereby linking Ca2+ signals to downstream synaptic signaling.
Specialized postsynaptic neuronal compartments where calcineurin and CaMKII are dynamically localized to distinct sites, enabling divergent synaptic plasticity responses.
A synaptic strengthening process driven here by CaMKII activity following large Ca2+ influxes through NMDARs.
A synaptic weakening process induced here by calcineurin in response to smaller Ca2+ influxes through NMDARs.
Calcium ions that act as the upstream signal controlling activation of calcineurin and CaMKII and determining whether potentiation or depression is induced.
Synaptic receptors that mediate Ca2+ influx into dendritic spines and thereby regulate activation of calcineurin and CaMKII.
Abbreviation for NMDA-type glutamate receptors, the receptor class through which Ca2+ influxes trigger divergent synaptic signaling responses.
A protein that interacts with calcineurin and CaMKII and contributes to their synaptic localization within dendritic spines.
A synaptic protein involved in localizing calcineurin and CaMKII within dendritic spines through protein-protein interactions.
A cytoskeletal-associated protein that participates in the structural localization of calcineurin and CaMKII in dendritic spines.
Localized calcium concentration gradients emanating from NMDAR mouths that are proposed to differentially position calcineurin and CaMKII and shape their signaling outputs.

Entry of calcium ions into the postsynaptic cell, described here as the initiating signal that activates CaMKII and drives downstream synaptic signaling relevant to learning and long-term potentiation.
A postsynaptic glutamate receptor that mediates Ca2+ influx and serves as a binding/anchoring site for CaMKII during synaptic activation.
A calcium/calmodulin-regulated kinase that is activated by Ca2+ influx, translocates to postsynaptic sites, and phosphorylates proteins involved in synaptic plasticity and long-term potentiation.
A calcium-bound signaling complex that promotes CaMKII binding to postsynaptic proteins, including the NMDA receptor, thereby supporting activity-dependent localization of CaMKII.
A group of proteins located at the postsynaptic density that interact with CaMKII and help anchor it at activated synapses.
Postsynaptic glutamate receptors that are phosphorylated by CaMKII as part of the signaling events supporting long-term potentiation.
Long-term potentiation, a synaptic plasticity process and physiological correlate of learning that depends on Ca2+-triggered CaMKII activation and postsynaptic clustering.
A higher-order cognitive outcome for which Ca2+ influx through NMDA receptors and CaMKII activation are described as crucial physiological correlates.
The property that only synapses receiving LTP-inducing activity undergo potentiation, supported by activity-dependent CaMKII accumulation at those synapses.
A synaptic stimulation pattern characterized by high-frequency activity that induces LTP and triggers Ca2+-dependent CaMKII clustering at specific synapses.
Activity-dependent accumulation of CaMKII at postsynaptic sites, enabling localized downstream signaling and contributing to synapse-specific LTP.
The process by which CaMKII is retained at postsynaptic locations through binding interactions with receptor-associated proteins, supporting localized signaling.
Activity-dependent modification of synaptic strength discussed as a broader functional context for postsynaptic CaMKII anchoring and clustering.
Disease outcomes mentioned as a potential context for the etiology and treatment implications of altered postsynaptic CaMKII signaling.

A persistent synaptic strengthening process induced during learning and proposed as a mechanism for memory storage. In this text, it is the central biological process being explained, with induction, synapse-specific localization, and later structural maintenance all attributed to CaMKII-dependent mechanisms.

A higher-level biological/behavioral process during which long-term potentiation occurs. It provides the physiological context for LTP induction and links synaptic plasticity to memory-related function.
The functional endpoint proposed to be supported by long-term potentiation. It represents the downstream cognitive outcome for which LTP is described as a probable mechanism.
The influx of calcium that occurs during LTP induction and activates CaMKII. It is an upstream signaling event essential for initiating the CaMKII-dependent cascade described in the abstract.

A key signaling kinase activated by calcium entry during LTP induction. It translocates to the synapse, binds NMDA-type glutamate receptors, phosphorylates AMPA-type glutamate receptor subunits, and later contributes structurally to synapse enlargement and strengthening.

The subcellular site where CaMKII translocates and exerts functional effects during LTP. It is the location of receptor interactions, phosphorylation events, and structural remodeling associated with synaptic potentiation.
Postsynaptic glutamate receptors that bind CaMKII in the synapse during LTP. They are part of the receptor complex involved in synapse-specific signaling and potentiation.
Glutamate receptor subunits whose principal and auxiliary components are phosphorylated by CaMKII to produce potentiation. They are central effectors of synaptic strengthening in LTP.
The receptor subunit components of AMPA-type glutamate receptors that are phosphorylated by CaMKII. Their modification is described as a mechanism producing synaptic potentiation.

Localized dendritic spine compartments where the described processes occur. They provide the spatial basis for synapse-specificity of LTP by restricting CaMKII-dependent signaling and structural changes to activated sites.
The strengthening of synaptic transmission produced by CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation of AMPA receptor subunits. It is the functional synaptic outcome underlying long-term potentiation in this text.
The property that LTP-related changes are restricted to stimulated synapses/spines rather than spreading broadly. It is explained here by the localization of CaMKII actions to stimulated spines.
The maintenance phase of LTP occurring after induction, during which CaMKII has a structural role. This stage is associated with synapse enlargement and strengthening rather than initial signaling.
A structural remodeling process attributed to CaMKII in the later stages of LTP. It reflects morphological stabilization and reinforcement of synaptic connections.
